newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel grabs for gold after tax blow clouds EMU.
newsitem.headline: Waigel grabs for gold after tax blow clouds EMU.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel made an unprecedented grab for Bundesbank gold on Thursday as he struggled to fill yawning gaps in his 1997 budget threatening to keep Germany from qualifying for Europe's single currency.

The powerful central bank, an outspoken critic of "creative accounting" to meet the Maastricht criteria, reacted with only a terse statement avoiding mention of Bonn's 18 billion mark ($10.6 billion) tax revenue shortfall announced on Thursday.

But Frankfurt bank analysts saw no chance for Germany, a pillar of the planned economic and monetary union (EMU), to end this year at or under the three percent budget deficit target the treaty sets out and Waigel has loudly defended.
"He will have to eat his words and say that a number slightly above the three percent will be fine too," remarked Stefan Schneider of Paribas in the German financial capital.

There was no sign of that as Waigel insisted in parliament in the morning and to journalists in the late afternoon that Germany would be in the front line of EMU in 1999 without any softening of the criteria taking place.

He said he wanted Bundesbank gold and currency reserves to be revalued from current low book prices to levels close to the normal market price, an accounting masterstroke that could create windfall profits of up to 40 billion marks for Bonn.
"Germany is not considering selling one ounce of gold or a single dollar," he declared, insisting Bonn was not cooking its books to qualify for Europe's single currency.
"I would accept this criticism if it were being used for the current budget, but it is not. It is going to be used to retire old debt," he insisted.

He also revealed Germany's record unemployment -- the main drag on his budget -- would average 4.3 million this year and cost the government up to 20 billion marks. Higher jobless levels automatically require more unemployment payments.

Waigel's mid-day helicopter dash to Frankfurt to talk gold with the Bundesbank sparked a lively debate in parliament, where opposition Social Democrats (SPD) demanded he quit. Germany's trade unions urged Bonn not to push through draconian savings to make up for the lost taxes.

On the government side, the liberal Free Democrats (FDP), Chancellor Helmut Kohl's pro-business junior coalition partner, said he was sure Bonn would continue with its plans to reduce overall tax levels despite the sharp shortfall in revenues.
"We must loosen the tax screw so that the economy can pick up again," general secretary Guido Westerwelle said.
The Federation of German Industry (BDI) urged a stepped-up privatisation drive to boost funds, especially by state and local authorities whose debts are also counted in the EMU sums.
It was not immediately clear how several of the stop-gap measures Waigel was considering would ease his budget woes.

His plan to sell off part of Bonn's large Deutsche Telekom share holdings could only be used to pay off old debt, which comes under a less critical Maastricht target setting debt at 60 percent of GDP.
Even if Bonn could turn the Bundesbank's 95 million ounces of underpriced gold into new revenue, it was not clear how it could use these funds to help meet the deficit target.
EU rules state gold sales from central banks can only be used to reduce government debt.

It was also not clear how the Bundesbank, whose laws would have to be changed, would react since a gold grab could prompt an unwanted expansion in money supply and encourage other EU members to fudge their qualifications for EMU.
"I cannot imagine the Bundesbank would like this very much, it would fire up the money printing presses," said Stefan Pelgrim, bond market analyst at Commerzbank in Frankfurt.
Deutsche Bank Research economist Hans-Juergen Meltzer said: "This definitely weakens Germany's position on Italy."
Bond markets seemed to sense Italy's chances for EMU may have just improved dramatically and sent the spread between Italian and German bonds to a record low of 148 basis points.

The tax commission that prepared the shortfall estimate said it also expected 1998 tax income for federal, state and local governments would be 31.6 billion marks below what Bonn had until now assumed.

In parliament, Waigel came out firmly against any weakening in the Maastricht criteria, saying: "Convergence determines the timetable, for every country." Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt firmly opposed a delay in launching the euro.
Afterwards, Kohl's majority defeated an opposition motion calling for an active jobs policy in the "stability pact" meant to guarantee the euro's value.
